articles.title: Trump says 2 new US bases coming to Greenland as deal signed
articles.summary: President Trump said on Tuesday that Greenland will host two new “major” U.S. military bases, expanding Washington’s footprint on the arctic island after months of tensions with Denmark. “We will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations. We’ll be building two very major military bases,” the president said…
articles.body:
President Trump said on Tuesday that Greenland will host two new “major” U.S. military bases, expanding Washington’s footprint on the arctic island after months of tensions with Denmark.

“We will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations. We’ll be building two very major military bases,” the president said during his speech at the United Nations .

The U.S. will reestablish a military base in south Greenland in Narsarsuaq and set up the other base on the eastern side of the island in Mestersvig, according to the 10-page agreement released later on Tuesday.

The U.S. military has approximately 150 service members stationed at Pituffik Space Base on the island’s northwest coast, according to U.S. defense officials. The Space Force-operated base supports missile defense, missile warning and space surveillance missions.

Under the agreement, the U.S. will be “allowed to modernize and expand its activities” at the Space Force base.

The U.S. can also establish additional military bases in Greenland and “strengthen its military operations or facilities,” according to the deal.

Denmark and Greenland will “review” U.S. requests to establish unmanned military installations in Greenland outside of current bases under the “accelerated governmental approval procedures,” the agreement said.

The U.S., Denmark and Greenland formally signed the security agreement that would bar any U.S. adversaries — China and Russia — from establishing a military presence on the arctic island or make “sensitive” investments without Washington’s approval.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the deal is “good” for all three sides and “can last forever.”

“Mr. President, you have been very clear. You don’t want adversaries to come too close. I fully agree, and with this deal, they are not,” Frederiksen said on Tuesday. “We are making sure that they will not be allowed to get any control or significant influence in Greenland, and we are making sure that more allies are present in the Arctic at the same time.”

The agreement came after months of ramped-up tensions after Trump’s repeated threats to take over Greenland, the semi-autonomous Danish territory.

Trump once threatened to use force against Greenland, and NATO members took the unprecedented step of sending troops there as a deterrent, claiming it was part of military exercises.

Germany, Sweden, France, Norway, the Netherlands and Finland all dispatched military personnel to the Arctic island in January, showing solidarity with Greenlanders.

“You go back way back in the line of presidents, and almost every president at least mentioned it,” Trump said on Tuesday. “But most of them just mentioned it. Some really wanted to make a deal, and never got done. But we’re getting it done.”

images.caption: President Donald Trump signs a security agreement with Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen during the United Nations General Assembly, Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026, at the UN headquarters. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

articles.title: 73 percent say AI firms not doing enough to prevent disaster: Survey
articles.summary: Nearly three-quarters of Americans are worried that artificial intelligence companies have not done enough to prevent the technology from causing serious harm, according to a new survey released Tuesday. The Reuters/Ipsos poll found 73 percent of respondents did not agree that the technology companies have implemented safeguards to prevent serious harm, sharing in the rising…
articles.body:
Nearly three-quarters of Americans are worried that artificial intelligence companies have not done enough to prevent the technology from causing serious harm, according to a new survey released Tuesday.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll found 73 percent of respondents did not agree that the technology companies have implemented safeguards to prevent serious harm, sharing in the rising concern over the rapidly developing technology.

Thirty-nine percent said AI has a negative impact on society, up from 36 percent last month, and the highest share since Reuters/Ipsos began asking the question in March.

Just 11 percent said they believe AI is making a positive impact.

The findings come after a series of warnings from AI researchers and industry leaders over the technology’s development.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called to slow the pace of AI development to allow further implementation of necessary safeguards, following several security breaches and AI models going rogue during testing.

A majority of the survey’s respondents, 55 percent, favored slowing the technology’s development and said doing so would be a good thing, compared with 13 percent who said it would be bad.

President Trump has instead sought to support rapid U.S. development of the technology in the AI race against China, announcing Saturday that he plans to create an “AI Force” and appoint an “AI czar.”

A panel of scientists backed by the United Nations warned Monday that existing safeguards may not keep pace as AI systems become more capable.

The Independent International Scientific Panel on AI pointed to an incident this summer during OpenAI cybersecurity testing in which AI models bypassed its restrictions and compromised parts of OpenAI’s and Hugging Face’s system without human authorization.

The panel called the incident one of the clearest real-world warnings of a potential path toward humans losing control of advanced AI systems.

Earlier this month, former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon warned that the increasingly powerful technology could eventually pose an existential threat to humanity.

“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Coxon wrote in a post on the social platform X, following his resignation from Anthropic.

His warning was echoed by Anthropic alignment science head Evan Hubbinger, who said , “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans.”

articles.title: As Trump and Xi meet, TD Cowen says the auto stock sell-off on Chinese car fears is 'overdone'
articles.summary: Wall Street thinks the odds of Chinese automakers breaking into the US market is low, but the US auto industry is taking no chances.
articles.body:
Wall Street thinks the odds of Chinese automakers breaking into the US market are low, but the US auto industry is taking no chances.

Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington on Wednesday for three days of talks, yet analysts expect small steps on trade and AI rather than breakthroughs . A bilateral trade truce expires in November, and the likeliest outcomes include possible tariff relief on a small set of less sensitive goods.

Cars are unlikely to be the main event. TD Cowen advised clients on Tuesday that a shift in US import policy at the summit is "very unlikely," even as it urged investors to prepare for the eventuality anyway.

"Most industry contacts have expressed similar views," senior analyst Itay Michaeli wrote, "w/ the typical caveat that regardless, we need to get prepared."

And the industry is gearing up for a fight. In a letter to Trump, a coalition led by the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, joined by the American Automotive Policy Council, dealer group NADA, and supplier association MEMA, urged the administration to "keep the door firmly shut to Chinese automakers seeking to sell, import, or manufacture vehicles inside the US.'

They credited Trump's 100% tariffs on Chinese vehicles and a Commerce Department rule barring Chinese connected-car software with keeping the US, unlike Europe, Australia, Southeast Asia, Mexico, and South America, from "grappling with a massive surge in cut-rate Chinese vehicles."

The fear is what happened north of the border in China, where Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney allowed a limited number of Chinese-made EVs into the country as part of a larger trade deal.

Given this backdrop, Michaeli and the TD Cowen team are gaming out scenarios.

The big question starts with how China's entry would be structured. The firm laid out the likely guardrails, such as Chinese automakers being forced in through minority-owned joint ventures (JVs) with domestic players and probably barred from building full-size trucks, products that generate the vast majority of the Big Three's North American profits.

Counterintuitively, the JVs could help the Detroit Three, per Michaeli. Such structures "might even prove EPS accretive given sizable D3 EV losses," Michaeli argued, "w/ Stellantis arguably having the most to gain given its lower NA [North America] EBIT starting point."

But the catch is that Big Three stock multiples could still suffer on the long-term risk that any initial restrictions eventually get lifted.

There are some beneficiaries in TD Cowen's view, such as EV suppliers and charging networks like ChargePoint ( CHPT ) and EVgo ( EVGO ), which would ride any acceleration in US EV adoption. Parts makers with existing ties to Chinese OEMs, including BorgWarner ( BWA ) and Aptiv ( APTV ), would be "better positioned" than most.

articles.title: Hegseth announces new Pentagon battlefield test for promotions to general
articles.summary: The Pentagon is altering the promotion process to get to the rank of general in an effort to “cut bureaucracy and demand true meritocracy” across the senior ranks, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Tuesday. In a video posted to the social platform X, Hegseth declared the Defense Department this year will roll out the Joint…
articles.body:
The Pentagon is altering the promotion process to get to the rank of general in an effort to “cut bureaucracy and demand true meritocracy” across the senior ranks, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Tuesday.

In a video posted to the social platform X, Hegseth declared the Defense Department this year will roll out the Joint Warfighter Evaluation, a new battlefield-style assessment for eligible colonels and Navy captains. The evaluation is intended to screen the officers aimed for one-star general or admiral on “their ability to fight, adapt, and win,” according to Hegseth.

“While the backbone of our military is our [non-commissioned officers] and our petty officers, victory depends on the commanders who lead them,” Hegseth said in the video.

“America needs warfighters who can master a chaotic battle space,” he added, later noting that commanders should be chosen by “proven competence, not paper credential.”

He likened the new evaluation to the “Louisiana Maneuvers,” a mass series of military exercises done directly before the U.S. entered World War II, during which roughly 400,000 troops conducted a wargame to evaluate America’s training, logistics and commanders.

Hegseth said such testing brought out such leaders as former President Dwight Eisenhower, a five-star Army general who planned and carried out the Allied assault on the coast of Normandy and the liberation of Western Europe; Army Gen. Omar Bradley the first chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff who eventually oversaw the U.S. military’s policy-making in the Korean War; and Adm. Chester Nimitz, who commanded Allied air, land, and sea in the Pacific theater during WWII.

The Joint Warfighter Evaluation “brings that standard to the modern multi-domain fight,” Hegseth said. “This evaluation is an objective equalizer. The scenario only cares about operational decisions under pressure.”

Hegseth said he had tasked Stu Scheller, the deputy chief of staff to the under secretary of defense for personnel and readiness, to lead the effort a year ago.

He did not go into details about what such testing will entail, but Fox News Digital reported that each military branch had its own version of the evaluation.

The Army will use a written assessment then a digital wargame; the Air Force and Space Force will require a two-hour online analysis test followed by a one-hour interactive simulation; the Navy will have officers travel to the Naval War College for a three-hour written assessment then a two-to-three-hour wargame; and the Marine Corps requires an eight-hour remote evaluation on an AI-enabled platform combining written assessments and situational judgment tests, according to the outlet.

The current system that is being phased out has promotion boards consider officers via their accumulated evaluations from their superiors throughout their careers.

articles.title: Vance-led task force set to remove 750K ObamaCare enrollees, citing fraud
articles.summary: The Trump administration is removing close to 760,000 people from Affordable Care Act (ACA) coverage due to allegedly fraudulent enrollment, Vice President Vance announced Tuesday. The cancellations would save an estimated $2.2 billion in taxpayer funds, officials said. “These are not real people. We’re not paying insurance for nonexistent ghosts,” Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator for…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is removing close to 760,000 people from Affordable Care Act (ACA) coverage due to allegedly fraudulent enrollment, Vice President Vance announced Tuesday.

The cancellations would save an estimated $2.2 billion in taxpayer funds, officials said.

“These are not real people. We’re not paying insurance for nonexistent ghosts,” Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), said during a White House press conference.

Oz and Vance said officials are planning to do “some additional verification” on about 419,000 people who they also suspect of being fraudulently enrolled.

“We’re actually making sure that the people receiving ObamaCare subsidies are actually entitled to receive them,” the vice president said.

Oz estimated that about 35 percent of people currently on the ObamaCare exchanges have never used their insurance.

The effort is being led by Vance’s White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud , which has been focusing much of its efforts on healthcare. The task force recently has been involved with White House efforts to withhold billions of dollars in Medicaid funding from Minnesota and California, alleging the states have not done enough to combat fraud.

“This is not about cutting off anybody from their benefits. It’s about cutting off fraudsters from stealing from these programs,” Vance said Tuesday.

Oz and Vance said they are not concerned about real people getting kicked off their plans as a result of the new crackdown because most of them didn’t file claims, have Social Security numbers or respond to outreach efforts.

“We are putting ourselves under an extraordinary burden of proof,” Vance said. “So those 750,000 people are people that we feel confident either don’t know that they’re enrolled in the program, aren’t using the program at all, are unaware of it or … are potentially phantom people who are enrolled against their will, or maybe they don’t even exist.”

The Congressional Budget Office previously estimated there were around 2.3 million people in 2025 who improperly claimed eligibility for ObamaCare tax credits because they intentionally overstated their income.

The administration is also putting a six-month moratorium on all new brokers and agents who signed individuals up for health insurance. Since January 2026, CMS has terminated more than 200 noncompliant agents and brokers, the agency said.

Ahead of November’s midterm elections, Republicans are looking for a healthcare affordability message and a counter to Democratic attacks that the expiration of enhanced ObamaCare subsidies and health cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act will drive up costs and increase the number of uninsured Americans.

ObamaCare enrollment grew sharply during the Biden administration but has fallen by several million people this year after Republicans in Congress allowed extra subsidies that helped people buy coverage to expire.

Costs soared due to the loss of enhanced subsidies, and many low-income people were faced with expensive plans that were previously free. Many either dropped coverage completely or shifted to less expensive plans with high deductibles.

About 19 million people are enrolled in health plans offered through the ACA’s exchanges, officials from the Health and Human Services Department said in June.

Administration officials and congressional Republicans contend the estimates of the number of people losing insurance have been overblown, and the losses that do happen are a result of cutting waste and fraud.

Democrats and the Biden administration were focused on boosting enrollment at all costs without putting enough safeguards in place to properly verify the people who signed up, they argued.

“This is what the fraud task force is all about,” the vice president said. “On the one hand, saving the American taxpayers money, and on the other hand, ensuring that these programs that are very important” are protected from fraud and abuse.

The Paragon Health Institute, an influential conservative think tank led by President Trump’s former economic aide Brian Blase, has focused much of its attention on ACA enrollment fraud.

The organization earlier this year found more than 6 million people were improperly enrolled in the health law’s exchanges in 2026. The report also argued taxpayers will improperly subsidize the ACA by nearly $25 billion.

The Democratic-aligned advocacy group Protect Our Care said the action is a “smokescreen” designed to kick more eligible people off their coverage and that the administration doesn’t actually care about fighting fraud.

The group noted that last May, the Trump administration reinstated 850 ObamaCare brokers and agents suspected of fraud.

“Families need coverage they can afford and count on when they get sick. Vance’s task force won’t accomplish that. It’s a smokescreen for an administration whose sole mission is to make it harder to get and stay covered but to shower billionaires with tax breaks instead,” Brad Woodhouse, Protect Our Care’s president, said in a statement.

articles.title: Rubio says Ukraine targeted US-linked ships, infrastructure
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that the Ukrainian military targeted U.S.-linked ships and infrastructure several times in recent months. “The one thing we are concerned about, however, is that over the last few months on a number of occasions American-linked ships, American oil supplies, have been targeted — probably not deliberately — but…
articles.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that the Ukrainian military targeted U.S.-linked ships and infrastructure several times in recent months.

“The one thing we are concerned about, however, is that over the last few months on a number of occasions American-linked ships, American oil supplies, have been targeted — probably not deliberately — but targeted nonetheless by Ukraine,” Rubio, who also serves as President Trump’s national security adviser, said during his appearance on “Fox & Friends.”

“So that’s something that needs to be addressed. We can’t have that happen,” he continued. “That’s why the president has wanted to end this war.”

The Pentagon did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment. The State Department declined to comment.

Rubio did not disclose any details about the attacks.

In late July, Vice President Vance asked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to stop striking oil tankers using the Caspian Pipeline Consortium’s (CPC) terminal in the Russian port city of Novorossiysk, The Financial Times (FT) reported .

The port has a terminal for a pipeline that carries crude oil from Kazakhstan.

The U.S. was “alarmed” that the strikes were further destabilizing oil markets and Ukraine agreed not to go after non-Russian ships that are not under Kyiv’s sanctions or target CPC infrastructure, according to FT.

Rubio’s remarks came hours before Zelensky and Trump are set to meet at the U.N. General Assembly in New York City. The Ukrainian leader met with CIA Director John Ratcliffe at an airport in Ireland on Monday, The Hill reported .

The secretary of state’s remarks also come as Zelensky has repeatedly asked the U.S. to provide Patriot interceptor missiles to help Ukraine defend against Russia’s massive missile attacks on the Eastern European country.

Earlier this year, Trump said the U.S. would allow Ukraine to co-produce Patriot missiles.

The president has called for the Russia-Ukraine war to end and on Monday acknowledged that Kyiv’s military strikes have hit Russian energy infrastructure hard, arguing Russia has lost control of its diesel oil industry.

articles.title: Richmond Fed's Barkin says supply shocks aren't proving short-lived, leaves door open to further rate hikes
articles.summary: Richmond Federal Reserve president Tom Barkin said Tuesday that stubborn inflation, recently fueled by higher oil prices and tariffs, drove the central bank'...
articles.body:
Richmond Federal Reserve president Tom Barkin said Tuesday that stubborn inflation, recently fueled by higher oil prices and tariffs, drove the central bank's decision to raise interest rates last week and leave the door open to further hikes.

"There was an argument that inflation would return to target on its own, without any additional help from the Fed," Barkin said in a speech in Baltimore. "One problem with that argument, of course, is that the 'passing' shocks aren't proving to be short-lived, or one-off events."

He noted new tariffs are still being imposed , the conflict in the Middle East is ongoing, and the build-out of AI continues to stress supply chains.

"These may pass in time, but I do expect it will take time," said Barkin. "In the interim, there is a risk that current elevated levels of inflation could affect future inflation… With inflation more than a percentage point above target, that's a problem."

Barkin underscored that inflation has been running above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years, and while oil has pushed up overall inflation this year, more than 60% of the Fed's preferred inflation measure — the Personal Consumption Expenditures index — is rising faster than 3% year over year.

Citing the Richmond Fed's monthly surveys, Barkin that noted growth in prices received has averaged 3.5% since late 2023, which is nearly double the average in the two years prior to the pandemic. The CFO Survey, which the Richmond Fed runs in collaboration with Duke University and the Atlanta Fed, showed firms expect to raise prices by 4.1% next year, more than double the 2019 average.

He noted the economy and the job market remain on solid footing and that while consumer spending is disproportionately driven by the well-off, those with fewer resources are still finding ways to maintain their spending.

On the business side, Barkin said companies are looking past the uncertainty that held them back last year because they can't afford to wait for certainty. Strong earnings give them courage, he said, while productivity improvements buy them wiggle room.

"The net of all this is more inflationary pressure. And that's why we needed to act," he said.

As for whether the central bank will need to raise rates further to bring inflation down, Barkin left the door open.

"We are committed to returning inflation sustainably to our 2% target. Last week's hike will help. Will additional hikes be required, and how many? We'll see," he said.

articles.title: San Francisco sues Trump Media for selling early access to Trump posts
articles.summary: ﻿The city is accusing Trump Media of facilitating insider trading.
articles.body: San Francisco is suing the Trump Media & Technology Group, the parent company behind Truth Social, for selling early access to President Donald Trump’s posts on the social media site. The lawsuit, filed today in California state court, alleges that the Truth API feed is a “corrupt business scheme” that violates both California’s Unfair Competition Law and federal ethics and anti-corruption laws that prohibit insider trading. White House spokesperson Davis Ingle recently called Truth Social the “most powerful and popular social media platform in the world.” While the latter part of that statement is objectively untrue based on any credible estimates — in fact, Truth Social traffic has declined over the last year — Trump often makes high-stakes announcements in his capacity as president on the platform, and his posts there have a clear effect on the global economy. To capitalize on this, Trump Media recently launched Truth API, a service that charges select customers $100,000 a month for early access to the 10 most influential accounts on Truth Social, including Trump’s and those of other White House officials. Trump Media’s interim CEO, Kevin McGurn, acknowledged as much in his announcement of Truth API, saying that “markets already move on Truth Social posts.” The San Francisco lawsuit cites several examples of this, some of which took place after the launch of Truth API. On August 21st, for example, Trump posted that the federal government was going to “lower the price of ground beef for working families” by exempting some ground beef imports from tariffs. When the market opened a few hours later, cattle futures declined significantly, according to the complaint. “Trump Media has unlawfully created, priced, marketed, and operated a commercial mechanism that knowingly and willfully facilitates Trump’s use of nonpublic information for private profit,” the complaint alleges. The San Francisco suit alleges that Truth API is a way of making the floundering Trump Media — which reported a net loss of more than $238 million earlier this year — profitable. Per his agreement with Trump Media, Truth Social has a six-hour exclusivity window on Trump’s posts, meaning he can’t post the same material elsewhere in that time frame. Even before the launch of Truth API, Trump’s Truth Social profile was extremely valuable for investors — so valuable that the company has sought to capitalize on it. The San Francisco complaint cites reports of hedge fund executives who say they feel pressured to buy the service even though they think it’s legally risky. “It’s a pay-to-play scheme for early access to the president’s market-moving government statements,” San Francisco city attorney David Chiu said in a Tuesday press conference. “In today’s markets, early access means millions of dollars. This business scheme has turned public trust into private property.” Beyond violating insider trading laws, the suit claims, Truth API disadvantages everyday investors by paywalling financially valuable information. Trump Media hasn’t disclosed its list of Truth API clients, but the company has said it plans on marketing the product to AI companies and large news organizations. The city has asked a judge to forbid Trump Media from offering Truth API or similar services, and to impose a fine of $2,500 per violation of California’s Unfair Competition Law. This isn’t the first time Trump has been sued over Truth API. In August, The Intercept and the Freedom of the Press Foundation filed a joint lawsuit in a New York federal court over the product, which it called “extraordinary, corrupt, and unconstitutional.” [Media:

articles.title: AI robot may stop your dog from barking while you're gone
articles.summary: WIM-Z's AI dog training robot uses on-device processing to detect barking and dispense treats autonomously, with field trials showing up to 83% reduction.
articles.body: If your dog starts barking the second you walk out the door, leaving home can come with a little extra guilt. That can happen whether you live in an apartment or a house. A pet camera can show you what is happening, but watching from your phone does little when your dog reacts to every sound outside or gets anxious when you are gone. WIM-Z wants to take a more active role. The small tracked robot uses on-device artificial intelligence to watch your dog and respond to certain behaviors. Once the robot is in position, it can identify your dog, detect barking and decide when to reward calmer behavior with a treat. You can also speak through the robot and drive it around your home from your phone. AI ROBOT FOR SENIORS CAN ALERT FAMILY AFTER A CALL FOR HELP Now WIM-Z has shared early field results, and its first customer units will make behavior and training decisions on their own while owners control where the robot moves. NEW! 🩺 Free CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI Saturday, September 26 at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed. Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com How the WIM-Z AI dog training robot works WIM-Z stands for Watchful Intelligent Mobile Zen. The robot measures about 11 inches tall and rides on rubber tank-style treads. Its camera turret can pan 270 degrees and tilt more than 120 degrees. A side cartridge holds up to 44 treats. Inside, WIM-Z uses a Raspberry Pi 5 with a Hailo-8 AI accelerator. The company says its onboard AI can identify individual dogs, classify barking and track a dog with its pan-and-tilt camera. Once WIM-Z detects barking, its behavior system can decide whether to intervene without waiting for you. The robot can then use a calming cue and dispense a treat when appropriate. However, there is an important limit. WIM-Z does not currently drive itself around your home looking for your dog. You control that movement through the app, or you can leave the robot in one location. WIM-Z also includes two-way audio. Its app can show behavior activity and optional highlight clips, giving you another way to see what happened while you were away. WIM-Z says barking dropped by as much as 83% WIM-Z recently released results from seven field trials conducted between May and September 2026. Six took place in homes around the New York metro area. One took place at a kennel in Jersey City. Across the trials, four hand-built robots logged 50 sessions and about 60 hours of use. WIM-Z says the system detected more than 2,100 barks. It also made 107 autonomous interventions and dispensed about 500 rewards. The biggest numbers came from two homes that ran repeat autonomous sessions over two to three weeks. In one home, barking fell from 161 barks per hour to 40, a 75% reduction. In the other, barking fell from 317 barks per hour to 53, an 83% reduction. WIM-Z also reported that more interventions ended with the dogs going quiet as the trials progressed. ROBOT DOG COULD DELIVER YOUR NEXT PACKAGE AND AN AD Why the reward-based approach stands out WIM-Z takes a gentler approach. Instead of using shocks, sprays or scolding, it relies on treats and calm cues to reinforce better behavior. That lines up with guidance from the American Veterinary Society of Animal Behavior, which recommends reward-based training and warns against aversive methods. The bigger question is whether the AI can read the situation well enough to respond appropriately. A dog barking at a delivery person is very different from one that is distressed because you left. WIM-Z has to recognize that difference and react at the right moment for the approach to work well. What WIM-Z can and cannot do on its own WIM-Z can handle the behavior side on its own. Its onboard AI can identify a dog, track it with the pan-and-tilt camera, detect barking, decide when to intervene and dispense a reward without you making each decision. What it cannot do yet is navigate your home on its own. You drive WIM-Z from room to room through the app, or you can leave it in one spot where your dog spends time. The first customer units will work this way, combining autonomous behavior and training features with owner-controlled movement. Full self-navigation, where the robot maps your home and goes looking for your dog by itself, remains on the company's roadmap and will not be included in the first units. So, WIM-Z can decide how to respond to your dog, but you still decide where the robot goes. What happens to your video and data? Any mobile robot with a camera and microphone deserves a privacy check before you let it roam around your living room. We asked WIM-Z exactly what happens to the information it collects. The company says all AI processing happens on the robot itself. That includes behavior detection, bark classification and decisions about when to intervene. No video is sent to the cloud for AI analysis. Some information can still leave the robot. Event data such as bark activity, behavior interventions, treat dispensing and battery status are stored on an Amazon Web Services relay server so it can appear in the app's activity history. If you connect remotely, live video and two-way audio stream through WIM-Z's relay using encrypted WebRTC technology. The company says these are live streams to your phone, not recordings, and they are not stored on its servers. Optional highlight clips work differently. Short selected clips can be uploaded for assembly and playback in the app, but WIM-Z says continuous footage is never uploaded. Owners can delete clips at any time or turn the feature off completely. The company says those clips are deleted within 90 days after an account is deleted. WIM-Z also told CyberGuy that it does not sell customer data. Customer footage is not used to train its AI models unless the owner explicitly opts in. When the robot is used only on local Wi-Fi without remote access, the company says nothing leaves the home. We have raised similar questions with other connected home robots because a camera that can move around your house gets access to very private spaces. Those answers give us a much clearer idea of how WIM-Z handles your information. Still, I would review the privacy controls before bringing any connected camera into my home. ONE-WHEELED AI SECURITY ROBOT COULD PATROL YOUR PROPERTY How much WIM-Z costs and when you can get one WIM-Z will cost $799 for the first production units. Right now, the company is taking a fully refundable $99 deposit to hold a spot. WIM-Z told CyberGuy it expects the first batch to ship from late Q4 2026 through Q1 2027. That means the first units could arrive between the end of 2026 and early 2027. The company also acknowledges that hardware schedules can slip. If WIM-Z has not shipped your unit by Q2 2027, it says your deposit will be refunded automatically. WIM-Z says the deposits are held through Stripe and are not placed in the company's operating account. The company says it has built five robots so far. Four are still being used in the field, while another is in Shenzhen, China, for production evaluation with a manufacturer. That gives you a pretty good sense of where things stand. WIM-Z is still in the early stages, so reserving one now means you are getting in before the product has been widely released and used in homes. What this means to you If your dog tends to bark or get restless when you leave, WIM-Z shows where pet tech may be headed next. Instead of simply alerting you that something is happening, the robot can respond while you are away by using a calming cue and rewarding your dog when it settles down. There is one thing to remember with the first version. WIM-Z will not roam around your house looking for your dog by itself. You will need to position it where your dog spends time or drive it remotely through the app. Still, I would not count on a robot to solve serious separation anxiety. The ASPCA says dogs with moderate or severe separation anxiety may need gradual behavior work with an experienced professional. For barking or mild restlessness, though, a robot that recognizes what your dog is doing and responds at the right time could be a useful extra set of eyes at home. The early results are interesting, but I want to see what happens when WIM-Z is tested with many more dogs in different homes. I also want to see how well the first production units perform once customers start using them. For now, WIM-Z has an interesting idea, some encouraging early numbers and a much clearer picture of what buyers will actually get. Kurt's key takeaways WIM-Z caught my attention because it tackles a problem pet cameras mostly leave in your hands. Seeing your dog bark from miles away can make you feel helpless. WIM-Z's onboard AI can make a training decision and reward calm behavior without waiting for you to step in. I also like that the first version keeps movement in your hands. You control where the robot goes, while the behavior and training system can operate on its own. Full self-navigation may come later. Keeping the AI processing on the robot means your video does not need to go to the cloud for behavior analysis. Remote features and optional highlight clips can still send some information outside your home, so you will want to understand those settings. At $799, I would still want to see more testing and hear from real customers once the first production units start shipping. But if WIM-Z can build on these early results, it could become a useful tool for dog owners who worry about what happens after they walk out the door. Would you trust an AI robot to decide when your dog needs a calming cue or treat while you are away? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: Hacking group ShinyHunters claims it breached the FBI, stole agents' and applicants' data | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The theft of agents' personal information could present a major counterintelligence threat, where agents and their families are extorted into cooperating with a foreign government.
articles.body:
ShinyHunters, a prolific cybercriminal group known for large-scale data theft and extortion, says it has breached the FBI and stolen data on thousands of agents and applicants. The hackers made the claim on their dark web leak site, which TechCrunch reviewed, saying they had stolen “sensitive data on almost all FBI agents and individuals who filed an application with the FBI for a job.”

404 Media first reported on the breach after receiving a sample of the stolen names, home addresses, and phone numbers of FBI agents and their spouses, and verifying a portion of the stolen data against public records. The hackers say their hack is “not financially motivated,” and are demanding that the FBI remove a report that they say contains false allegations about the group.

The independent publication said the hackers breached an Oracle PeopleSoft server, often used by human resources and recruiters to store job applicants’ personal information, then pivoted to breach an Amazon-hosted government cloud storing the agents and applicants’ data.

ShinyHunters told the publication that they took terabytes of data but did not say what they would do with the information if the FBI does not take down its published report. The stolen data could present a major counterintelligence threat, in which hackers and overseas spies use the information to coerce or extort FBI agents and their families into cooperating with a foreign government.

The hackers reportedly defaced the FBI’s jobs site, which showed at the time of publication that the portal was “currently down for maintenance.” The site also said that the FBI’s special agent applicant portal was also down.

The FBI did not respond to a request for comment about the incident on Tuesday, and neither did the ShinyHunters hackers.

This is the second known breach of an FBI system this year after unidentified hackers broke into one of the agency’s systems for managing real-time wiretaps and foreign intelligence-gathering warrants, which could have identified targets of the agency’s surveillance. Separately, FBI director Kash Patel also had his personal email account hacked and leaked by an Iran-backed hacking group called Handala in retaliation for U.S.-led strikes against Iran.

articles.title: Trump backs diesel export ban; Bessent says admin ‘examining that’
articles.summary: The Trump administration is considering a ban on exports of diesel as high prices of the fuel put a crunch on American agriculture and trucking. Asked Tuesday whether he was considering a ban on diesel exports, as some Republican lawmakers have called for in recent days, President Trump said, “I’ve called for that, too.” “I’ve…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is considering a ban on exports of diesel as high prices of the fuel put a crunch on American agriculture and trucking.

Asked Tuesday whether he was considering a ban on diesel exports, as some Republican lawmakers have called for in recent days, President Trump said, “I’ve called for that, too.”

“I’ve said, ‘Let’s not send out the diesel.’ We make a lot of diesel,” Trump said during a bilateral meeting with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

“I’ve called for it within my people. I’ve been talking about it,” he added, then called upon Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to expound on the issue.

“We’re examining that, whether it’s feasible in terms of the overall refining capacity and whether a full or partial ban would work,” Bessent said.

It’s not clear how soon, if ever, the administration could come to a decision on whether to actually restrict exports of diesel. The White House declined to answer follow-up questions from The Hill, referring back to the president’s remarks.

Over the weekend, several Republicans, particularly those from agriculture-heavy states such as Iowa, expressed support for barring diesel exports as prices hit record levels .

The option divides GOP lawmakers, with members from more oil-producing states dismissing the idea as “a gimmick.”

The average price of diesel, which powers tractors and trucks alike, was averaging about $6.53 cents per gallon on Tuesday, according to AAA , up about 93 cents from this time last month and $2.84 from this time last year.

Experts recently told The Hill that high diesel prices were due to both higher prices of oil — stemming from instability over the U.S.-Iran conflict — and damage to refineries that turn oil into fuels caused by both the U.S.-Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars.

articles.title: Netanyahu Attacks Mamdani on Social Media Ahead of UN Speech
articles.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attacked New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani in a video Tuesday, escalating a feud with one of his most prominent US crit...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attacked New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani in a video Tuesday, escalating a feud with one of his most prominent US critics as he travels to the United Nations General Assembly.

"Shame on you, Mr. Mamdani," Netanyahu said in the video posted to social media, accusing the mayor of supporting Hamas and "inciting" violence against Jewish New Yorkers. He said he would use his UN address to "tell the truth about our heroic soldiers, and I'm going to tell the truth about you."

Mamdani called Netanyahu's accusations false, pointing to the International Criminal Court arrest warrant for the Israeli leader over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.

"We all know that what the prime minister has said in that video is not true," Mamdani told reporters. He called Netanyahu "the architect of horrific genocide against Palestinians" and said Israeli forces killed an 11-year-old boy in a designated safe zone in Gaza days earlier.

Israel rejects accusations of genocide, saying its war in Gaza was a legitimate response to the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas, in which militants killed about 1,200 people and took roughly 250 hostage. Israel's military campaign has left more than 73,000 people dead, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry.

The confrontation is the latest in a months-long dispute between the two leaders, and comes a day after Mamdani and President Donald Trump appeared together at Gracie Mansion, where Trump praised the mayor saying he's "got great potential."

Mamdani backed away in July from a pledge to enforce the ICC warrant against Netanyahu, acknowledging that as mayor he lacks the legal authority to do so. Heads of state traditionally have diplomatic immunity while in the US on official business, and the US isn't a party to the ICC.

Mamdani has continued his criticism of the Israeli leader, labeling him a war criminal who "is not welcome in New York City."

Netanyahu said Sunday on Fox News that he would attend the General Assembly despite the dispute, accusing Mamdani of promoting "bogus charges," dividing New Yorkers and "fomenting hate."

"I intend to come and speak the truth, speak for Israel and for the Israeli-American alliance from the podium of the United Nations," Netanyahu said.

articles.title: Collins urges White House not to move forward with NIH grant proposal
articles.summary: Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, on Tuesday urged Trump administration officials to not proceed with an executive order that would give the White House political control over scientific grants at the National Institutes of Health (NIH). In a letter to Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought and NIH…
articles.body:
Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, on Tuesday urged Trump administration officials to not proceed with an executive order that would give the White House political control over scientific grants at the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

In a letter to Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought and NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya, Collins noted that the stopgap government funding bill passed earlier this month blocked a similar proposal that sought to give political appointees broader authority over approving federal research grants to ensure they meet the president’s priorities.

The proposal to establish a political review board for NIH grants would undermine “the federal government’s objective of funding biomedical research projects based on scientific merit and value rather than political ideology,” Collins wrote.

Collins has pushed back against White House efforts to exert greater control over NIH funding. Earlier this year, Collins opposed a 15 percent cap on indirect research costs.

She also issued a strong statement blasting the proposed order on Monday, along with the top Democratic appropriators Sen. Patty Murray (Wash.) and Rep. Rosa DeLauro (Conn.).

Collins in her letter Tuesday highlighted how the current NIH grantmaking process has helped drive research breakthroughs for illnesses like Alzheimer’s disease, Type 1 diabetes and cancer.

“Your proposal to establish a new committee to review NIH grants risks undermining the Congressionally-mandated peer review process that all NIH grants must undergo before they are approved for federal funding,” Collins wrote. “The rigor of the peer review process is key to NIH’s success” and has contributed to 174 scientists either working at or funded by NIH winning Nobel Prizes.

“If the administration seeks additional reforms of NIH, I urge you to submit a legislative proposal to Congress rather than pursue an executive order,” Collins continued.

articles.title: Bipartisan senators press Blanche for guidance on automated license plate readers
articles.summary: A bipartisan pair of senators are pressing the head of Department of Justice to provide guidance to state and local law enforcement agencies to prevent the misuse of automated license plate readers (ALPRs) as backlash against the technology grows across the country. In a letter sent Monday, Sens. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) and Katie Britt (R-Ala.)…
articles.body:
A bipartisan pair of senators are pressing the head of Department of Justice to provide guidance to state and local law enforcement agencies to prevent the misuse of automated license plate readers (ALPRs) as backlash against the technology grows across the country.

In a letter sent Monday, Sens. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) and Katie Britt (R-Ala.) urged Attorney General Todd Blanche, urging him to issue the guidance and disclose details about any DOJ use of ALPRs.

“While law enforcement agencies around the country appropriately use ALPR for legitimate public safety purposes including the investigation of violent crime and the location and recovery of missing and abducted persons, misuse of these systems undermines the public’s confidence in the technology,” the senators wrote.

The lawmakers said they request “information about the DOJ funding and oversight of such systems to prevent such misuse and ensure compliance with applicable federal statutes and regulations.”

The senators mention Flock Safety, which became mired in controversy earlier this year for its network of more than 120,000 cameras across the country.

Flock’s plate readers not only record license plate numbers, but specific details about a car to create what the company calls a “vehicle signature.” These details include the make, model and color of the car along with unique features like bumper stickers, decals, and accessories. The company does not use biometric data or facial recognition.

A series of news reports in recent months have uncovered multiple instances of law enforcement misusing Flock or other ALPRs.

An investigation by The Washington Post found that more than 50 officers had been accused, charged with or convicted of misusing Flock or other license plate readers to spy on exes or romantic interests.

“We are deeply concerned about the misuse of ALPR systems and believe that appropriate safeguards are necessary to protect against unauthorized access and abuse, including by individuals who might misuse the technology to stalk and harass their victims,” Britt and Warnock wrote.

“We also want to ensure that funding of these technologies is paired with appropriate oversight to ensure that the funding is not used to facilitate such abuse,” they added.

From local to federal government, policymakers across the aisle have increasingly sounded the alarm about the technology’s privacy implications this year.

The issue gained gained recent attention on the right, stoking privacy-conscious conservatives despite the party’s support for law and order.

The extent of federal agencies’ use of ALPRs is unclear. According to a report from the U.S. Government Accountability Office last year stated Customs and Border Protection (CBP), Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Secret Service disclosed agreements to query or view information from third-party automated license plate readers.

In addition to funding, the senators asked Blanche to answer what “grant oversight and accountability” mechanisms the DOJ has in place to address potential misuse, and whether the agency has policies on the collection, storage and access to ALPR data.

The lawmakers’ letter was sent just two days before the Senate’s Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism hosts a hearing on Flock’s “nationwide AI surveillance network.”

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) said he invited the CEOs of Flock and other ALPR firms to testify, though none were listed on the witness list as of Tuesday afternoon.

The Hill reached out to the DOJ and Flock for further comment.

articles.title: Lawsuit targets ‘medically frail’ Medicaid work requirement exemption
articles.summary: A new lawsuit is challenging how the Trump administration plans to exempt medically frail people from Medicaid work requirements. Medicaid enrollees, alongside several major health care advocacy organizations and the city of Columbus, Ohio, said the administration’s final rule implementing work requirements is not what Congress intended. They argue the rule narrowly defines who qualifies…
articles.body:
A new lawsuit is challenging how the Trump administration plans to exempt medically frail people from Medicaid work requirements.

Medicaid enrollees, alongside several major health care advocacy organizations and the city of Columbus, Ohio, said the administration’s final rule implementing work requirements is not what Congress intended.

They argue the rule narrowly defines who qualifies for the law’s medical frailty exclusion, putting people with serious physical and mental health conditions at risk of losing Medicaid because of new reporting and verification requirements, even though Congress categorically excluded medically frail people from the requirements.

The coalition is asking a federal court in Maryland to vacate the rule, alleging it’s “arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law.” The suit also alleges violations of the Administrative Procedure Act, the law governing how regulations are issued.

The rule, issued in July, is meant to guide 42 states and the District of Columbia in carrying out the work rules implemented by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. GOP lawmakers and administration officials have described the policy as a way to combat waste, fraud and abuse in the Medicaid program.

The work requirements are set to take effect in January. Beneficiaries who are part of the Medicaid expansion population must work or volunteer at least 80 hours per month, attend school at least part time or participate in job training.

Expansion states are responsible for ensuring working-age recipients are meeting the requirement unless they are disabled, caring for young children, or have a serious health condition.

The rule implicitly links the definition of medical frailty to a person’s ability to work. To qualify for an exemption, a person must demonstrate that their condition prevented them from meeting the work requirement.

However, chronically ill people and advocates have expressed concern over how they’re supposed to prove they are too sick to work.

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services recently issued new guidance allowing states to use a “tier system” to reduce administrative burden.

The tiered system would be established based on available diagnostic coding and data sets. So instead of merely setting up a list of certain diagnoses that could qualify a person for an exemption, states can also put the conditions into tiers.

For instance, Tier 1 would mean a diagnosis alone is enough to show that a person won’t be able to meet the work requirement. A Tier 2 condition could mean an individual is medically frail but additional information is needed to determine if the condition is serious enough to prevent the person from working.

“Congress created the medical frailty exclusion to protect people with serious health needs, but the administration’s rule turns that protection into yet another obstacle people must overcome,” Jane Perkins, litigation director at the National Health Law Program, which is representing some of the plaintiffs, along with legal advocacy group Democracy Forward.

“The statute exempts the medically frail from work requirements and does not authorize CMS to re-introduce it through the backdoor with the new rule. This rule puts access to care and, in some cases, people’s lives at risk,” Perkins said.

The lawsuit is the latest attempt to challenge the work requirements. In June, about two dozen states sued the Trump administration over the “medically frail” definition. A federal judge in July denied the states’ request to block the rule while the lawsuit is agued.

articles.title: Trump’s ‘Lavish Welcome’ for Xi Slammed by Key GOP Senator
articles.summary: Senate Armed Services Chairman Roger Wicker sharply criticized Donald Trump for the manner in which he plans to host Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washingt...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Senate Armed Services Chairman Roger Wicker sharply criticized Donald Trump for the manner in which he plans to host Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington this week, marking a significant public break from a key member of the president's own party just ahead of the high-stakes summit.

"Quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States of America, based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party," Wicker said in a Senate floor speech Tuesday.

Xi's trip marks his first visit to Washington in over a decade. Trade and the US-China race over artificial intelligence are expected to dominate the summit.

Tech leaders including Meta Platforms Inc.'s Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg, Amazon.com Inc. founder Jeff Bezos, Tesla Inc. CEO Elon Musk, Alphabet Inc. chief Sundar Pichai, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Qualcomm Inc. head Cristiano Amon are all expected to attend a state dinner on Thursday.

"As we know, a proper state visit requires a proper state dinner," Wicker said in his remarks. "Again, I would not have scheduled such a thing. But as guests converse over the meal, the president might inquire about the purposes of China's massive military build-up, or about China's clear support for Iran."

Wicker also urged Trump to advocate for the Uyghur people and discuss other human rights issues, as well as Taiwan.

"Our commander in chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America," he said.

articles.title: Kagan steers Supreme Court clear of high-profile surrogacy fight
articles.summary: Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan declined a surrogate’s emergency bid on Tuesday to intervene in her custody fight that drew national attention after the biological parents’ told her to get an abortion and she left for Texas instead. McKenna West, the surrogate, sought to lift a parentage judgment in favor of the couple issued in a California…
articles.body:
Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan declined a surrogate’s emergency bid on Tuesday to intervene in her custody fight that drew national attention after the biological parents’ told her to get an abortion and she left for Texas instead .

McKenna West, the surrogate, sought to lift a parentage judgment in favor of the couple issued in a California court, where they reside. West said the case needed to be litigated in Alaska, where she lives.

Kagan received the emergency request by default and denied it in a one-sentence order without explanation. It keeps the Supreme Court out of the high-profile dispute, which implicates three states and broaches broader issues surrounding abortion and surrogacy.

Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar, the couple, had demanded West abort the then-unborn child under their surrogacy agreement. Doctors had diagnosed the fetus with hypoplastic left heart syndrome. The serious condition leaves the left side of the heart underdeveloped and unable to properly pump blood throughout the body. Doctors recommended three after-birth surgeries as the standard treatment for the condition, court filings show.

West refused an abortion and instead left Alaska for Texas , where she gave birth to the boy on Aug. 12. The surrogate tried to appeal an order the couple secured in California’s courts declaring them the legal parents. West said that has meant she is being denied any information or control over the child.

Kagan manages emergency matters arising from California by default. She could’ve referred the matter to the full court for a vote but instead chose to act alone.

West was represented by a legal team that includes Alliance Defending Freedom, a conservative Christian legal group that has notched wins in many high-profile Supreme Court cases. They argued the case needed to be litigated in Alaska, not California.

articles.title: Trump’s Grip on GOP Slips as Midterm Election Anxiety Sets In
articles.summary: As Donald Trump took an aggressive stance on the global stage at the United Nations on Tuesday, several Senate Republicans were breaking from the president b...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- As Donald Trump took an aggressive stance on the global stage at the United Nations on Tuesday, several Senate Republicans were breaking from the president back in Washington.

The GOP backlash, which has been simmering below the surface throughout Trump's second term as lawmakers privately grumbled he hasn't focused enough on affordability issues, burst into public view as a rapid succession of Republicans challenged Trump on everything from the Iran war to the president's "lavish" summit this week with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Republicans have long been loathe to openly criticize the president, who has wielded an uncommonly strong hold over his party and retains long memories about who has crossed him. Back in May, eight Indiana state lawmakers who defied Trump on a redistricting plan faced their primary voters, and only two won. The president that month similarly ended Texas Senator John Cornyn's political career by backing Ken Paxton's primary challenge instead.

So confident is the president of his singular electoral magnetism that his rallying cry at campaign events from Texas to North Carolina has been to call on his supporters to vote as if he's on the ballot in November.

Yet those same Republican lawmakers who held tight with Trump through the primaries are now facing a general election environment and a very different electorate. They now have to contend not just with GOP voters, but Democrats who've always opposed the president, as well as disaffected independents who've drifted from Trump over economic concerns.

Retail gasoline prices are up. So is diesel. The cost of financing government debt has risen since the Iran war began, driving up the cost of mortgages, credit cards and consumer debt. And a confident White House that has unapologetically pursued all of its priorities at once, from tariffs to getting Trump's name on the Kennedy Center, is increasingly seen as unfocused on the costs Americans pay to go about their daily lives.

Trump's reservoir of support began to crack last week, when Florida Republican Maria Elvira Salazar cut a video telling Trump that his immigration crackdowns have gone "too far," as she battles to retain her House seat in a Miami-area district heavily impacted by the administration's deportation policies.

articles.title: Bengaluru firm emerges L1 for army’s 600 software-defined radio order
articles.summary: News News: BENGALURU: Bengaluru-based defence equipment manufacturer Alpha Design Technologies has emerged as the lowest bidder (L1) for an Indian Army requireme.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Bengaluru-based defence equipment manufacturer Alpha Design Technologies has emerged as the lowest bidder (L1) for an Indian Army requirement for 600 indigenous man-pack software-defined radios (SDR).Alpha Design, controlled by Adani Group, and defence PSU Bharat Electronics Ltd (BEL) were the two companies to qualify the technical evaluation. “The third competitor, a joint venture involving Astra and Rafael, did not technically qualify and its commercial bid was not opened,” a source told TOI.The technical evaluation included user trials, field trials, high-altitude trials and desert trials. All three companies had submitted techno-commercial bids, but only those that cleared the technical evaluation were considered for the commercial stage.The commercial bids were opened on Monday. The immediate order — expected to be worth around Rs 100 crore — is part of a much larger requirement for man-pack radios. While Alpha has tie-ups with foreign companies, the SDRs have algorithms that were built in-house.“While the company has imported components and has technology partnerships, the internal software was developed indigenously in accordance with the Government of India’s requirement in the RFP. That was one of the conditions by the Army and the firm wouldn’t qualify otherwise,” another source said.According to sources, the Army’s next requirement is for approximately 16,000 sets, while the overall requirement could be around 50,000 man-pack radios over the next five to 10 years.The Army is expected to look at multiple firms again for the 16,000 sets, but any party that wins that bid may be considered for larger orders in the future given that compatibility would become key. “Whoever wins the 16,000 is mostly likely to be the single vendor for the remaining ones, because the Army cannot change the algorithms and encryption and all that,” the source said.The larger requirement is also linked to interoperability between different versions of software-defined radios. The system comprises man-pack, handheld and armoured fighting vehicle (AFV) versions. Alpha had earlier received an order for 400 AFV radios, which were fitted on T-72 tanks, primarily in the Leh-Ladakh region.Radio systems built by different organisations or firms use different software algorithms and encryption, creating interoperability issues between them. In other words, a man pack radio cannot speak to a tank radio, a handheld radio cannot speak to a tank radio when they are all not designed using the same systems.
